newsitem.title: USA: "Cats" breaks Broadway record for longevity.
newsitem.headline: "Cats" breaks Broadway record for longevity.

text.p: The musical "Cats" made history on Thursday night as the longest-running show in Broadway history.

The giddy audience at the record-breaking 6,138th performance of Andrew Lloyd Webber's hit musical -- about a pack of felines learning to transcend their catty ways in a quest for moral purr-fection -- rewarded the 22 actors and actresses with several standing ovations.

Dozens of the 195 former "Cats" cast members attended the historic show, cheering their former characters as they took center stage and crowding the aisles to sing along to the finale, "The Ad-Dressing of Cats".
"It was everything we ever dreamed it would be," said actor David Hibbard, who plays the raunchy rocker cat, Rum Tum Tugger.
"Cats" surpassed "A Chorus Line" on Thursday as the longest-running production ever in the famed entertainment district.
The performance was followed by an outdoor laser show projected onto the marquee of Broadway's Winter Garden Theatre, where "Cats" opened on Oct. 7, 1982.
Mayor Rudolph Giuliani spoke to the crowd and proclaimed June 19, 1997 as "Cats' Day" in New York.
"What you do here on Broadway draws more people to New York than anything else," he said to the show's creators.
Since "Cats" opened on Broadway, more than 8.25 million people have seen the show, which won seven 1983 Tonys, including Best Musical.
Before the show, "Cats" creators offered their explanations for the production's longevity.

"The key is the poetry," said Lloyd Webber, adding that his mother used to read him "Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats" by T.S. Eliot, the inspiration for the musical which premiered in London in 1981.
"There's a mystery about cats worldwide. There's a love of the domestic cat and an interest in cats as ritual creatures and religious icons," said director Trevor Nunn.
"It's a tale of hope," said Marlene Danielle, who has played Bombalurina, the dignified cat in the New York production since its opening.
The show has used a ton of yak hair for wigs, 5,782 knee pads to protect its 231 performers and more than 48,000 condoms to protect body microphones from perspiration.
After the performance, the perspiring actors, the proud creators of "Cats" and select admiring fans made their way to an extravagant party at the Grand Ballroom of the New York Hilton.
Casts and crews from all the shows now playing on Broadway were invited, producers said.
